facts.statement: Richard Owen named and described the genus Scelidosaurus in 1859 following initial fossil finds in the 1850s.
facts.quote: After initial finds in the 1850s, comparative anatomist Richard Owen named and described Scelidosaurus in 1859.

facts.statement: Only the species Scelidosaurus harrisonii, named by Owen in 1861, is currently considered valid, despite a proposal of another species in 1996.
facts.quote: Only one species, Scelidosaurus harrisonii named by Owen in 1861, is considered valid today, although one other species was proposed in 1996.

facts.statement: Scelidosaurus lived during the Early Jurassic epoch, specifically the Sinemurian to Pliensbachian ages, approximately 191 million years ago.
facts.quote: Scelidosaurus lived during the Early Jurassic epoch, during the Sinemurian to Pliensbachian ages around 191 million years ago

facts.statement: Fossils of Scelidosaurus have been found in the Charmouth Mudstone Formation near Charmouth in Dorset, England.
facts.quote: Its fossils have been found in the Charmouth Mudstone Formation near Charmouth in Dorset, England

facts.statement: Scelidosaurus was approximately 4 meters long.
facts.quote: Scelidosaurus was about 4 m long.

facts.statement: Scelidosaurus was largely quadrupedal and fed on low scrubby plants, which were bitten off by its small, elongated head and processed in a large gut.
facts.quote: It was a largely quadrupedal animal, feeding on low scrubby plants, the parts of which were bitten off by the small, elongated head to be processed in the large gut.

facts.statement: Scelidosaurus was lightly armoured with long horizontal rows of keeled oval scutes extending along its neck, back, and tail.
facts.quote: Scelidosaurus was lightly armoured, protected by long horizontal rows of keeled oval scutes that stretched along the neck, back and tail.

facts.statement: While some estimates place Scelidosaurus at 4 meters long, Gregory S. Paul estimated its length at 3.8 meters and weight at 270 kg in 2010.
facts.quote: Some scientists have estimated a length of 4 metres (13 ft). In 2010, Gregory S. Paul gave a body length of 3.8 metres (12.5 ft) and a weight of 270 kg.

facts.statement: The head of Scelidosaurus was small, elongated, and approximately twenty centimeters long.
facts.quote: The head of Scelidosaurus was small, about twenty centimetres long, and elongated.

facts.statement: The skull of Scelidosaurus was low in side view, triangular in top view, and longer than it was wide, resembling earlier ornithischians.
facts.quote: The skull was low in side view and triangular in top view, longer than it was wide, similar to that of earlier ornithischians.

facts.statement: Scelidosaurus is considered one of the oldest and most primitive thyreophorans, though its exact placement within the group has been debated for nearly 150 years.
facts.quote: One of the oldest known and most "primitive" of the thyreophorans, the exact placement of Scelidosaurus within this group has been the subject of debate for nearly 150 years.

facts.statement: Current evidence suggests Scelidosaurus is the most derived of known basal thyreophorans, being either closely related to Ankylosauria or to the Stegosauria+Ankylosauria clade.
facts.quote: Today most evidence suggests that Scelidosaurus is the most derived of the known basal thyreophorans, either closely related to Ankylosauria or Stegosauria+Ankylosauria.

facts.statement: The first modern diagnosis of Scelidosaurus was provided by David Bruce Norman in 2020.
facts.quote: The first modern diagnosis was provided by David Bruce Norman in 2020.

facts.statement: In 2020, Norman concluded that a specific brow ridge bone in Scelidosaurus was a fused palpebral bone.
facts.quote: In 2020, Norman concluded that it was a fused palpebral bone.

facts.statement: The torso of Scelidosaurus was relatively flat in side view and taller than wide, unlike the vertically compressed bodies of ankylosaurs.
facts.quote: The torso was relatively flat in side view, however, despite the belly being broad, it was not extremely vertically compressed as with ankylosaurs but taller than wide.

facts.statement: The tail of Scelidosaurus was relatively short and quickly tapering, likely representing about half of the animal's total body length.
facts.quote: The quickly tapering tail was relatively short, probably representing about half of body length.

facts.statement: Large numbers of ossified tendons stiffened the hip area and tail base of Scelidosaurus.
facts.quote: The hip area and tail base were stiffened by large numbers of ossified tendons.

facts.statement: The coracoid bone of Scelidosaurus was circular in side view.
facts.quote: The coracoid was circular in side view.

facts.statement: The elements of the forelimb of Scelidosaurus were generally moderately long, straight, and stout.
facts.quote: The elements of the forelimb were generally moderately long, straight and stout.

facts.statement: The claws of Scelidosaurus were flat, hoof-shaped, and curved inward.
facts.quote: The claws were flat, hoof-shaped and curved to the inside.

facts.statement: The osteoderms of Scelidosaurus varied in size and shape, with most being oval plates featuring a high keel on the outside, highest point positioned toward the rear.
facts.quote: The osteoderms of Scelidosaurus ranged in both size and shape. Most were smaller or larger oval plates with a high keel on the outside, the highest point of the keel positioned more to the rear.

facts.statement: The skull of Scelidosaurus featured bony outgrowths covering much of its surface, along with plates encircling the eye socket and a pair of horns extending upward and backward from the rear.
facts.quote: The skull consists of bony outgrowths covering much of its surface, accompanied by separate bony plates encircling the upper portion of the eye socket and forming a pair of horns that extend upward and backward from the rear of the skull.

facts.statement: The neck of Scelidosaurus had two rows of large scutes on each side.
facts.quote: The neck had at each side two rows of large scutes.

facts.statement: Compared to later ankylosaurs, Scelidosaurus was lightly armored, lacking continuous plating, spikes, or a pelvic shield.
facts.quote: Compared to the later Ankylosauria, Scelidosaurus was lightly armoured, without continuous plating, spikes or pelvic shield.

facts.statement: Some recent specimens of Scelidosaurus show osteoderms with keels that resemble thorns or spikes.
facts.quote: Some of the latest specimens found show partly different osteoderms including scutes on which the keel is more like a thorn or spike.

facts.statement: Very small, flat bone granules measuring 5-10 millimeters were perhaps distributed within the skin between the large scutes of Scelidosaurus.
facts.quote: Between the large scutes, very small (5-10 millimetres [0.2-0.4 in]) flat "granules" of bone were perhaps distributed within the skin.

facts.statement: James Harrison discovered Scelidosaurus fossils in the Black Ven cliffs near Charmouth and Lyme Regis in England during the 1850s.
facts.quote: During the 1850s, quarry owner James Harrison of Charmouth, West Dorset of England found fossils from the cliffs of Black Ven between Charmouth and Lyme Regis

facts.statement: In 1858, James Harrison and Henry Norris sent fragmentary limb bones to Professor Richard Owen at the British Museum in London.
facts.quote: In 1858, Norris and Harrison sent some fragmentary limb bones to Professor Richard Owen of the British Museum (Natural History), London

facts.statement: The initial bones sent to Richard Owen included a left thighbone identified as specimen GSM 109560.
facts.quote: Among them was a left thighbone, specimen GSM 109560

facts.statement: Richard Owen named the genus Scelidosaurus in 1859 within an entry for the Encyclopædia Britannica.
facts.quote: In 1859, Owen named the genus Scelidosaurus in an entry about palaeontology in the Encyclopædia Britannica

facts.statement: The name Scelidosaurus was chosen because of the animal's strong hind legs.
facts.quote: The name was inspired by the strong development of the hind leg

facts.statement: Additional fossils, including a knee joint, a claw, a juvenile specimen, and a skull, were sent to Owen and described in 1861.
facts.quote: Afterwards Harrison sent a knee joint, a claw (GSM 109561), a juvenile specimen and a skull to Owen, that were described in 1861

facts.statement: Richard Owen described a nearly complete skeleton containing the skull in 1863.
facts.quote: The skull later was revealed to be part of a nearly complete skeleton, that was described by Owen in 1863

facts.statement: In 1888, Richard Lydekker designated a knee joint (specimen NHMUK PV 39496) as the type specimen for Scelidosaurus.
facts.quote: In 1888, Richard Lydekker while cataloguing the NHMUK fossils, designated some of the hindlimb fragments described in 1861, specimen NHMUK PV 39496 consisting of a lower part of a femur and an upper part of the tibia and fibula, together forming a knee joint, as the type specimen

facts.statement: Bernard Newman discovered in 1968 that the knee joint originally selected as the type specimen actually belonged to a theropod dinosaur.
facts.quote: this was not discovered until 1968 by Bernard Newman

facts.statement: In 1994, the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature designated specimen NHMUK PV R 1111 as the new lectotype of Scelidosaurus.
facts.quote: In 1994 the ICZN reacted positively, in Opinion 1788 deciding that the skull and skeleton, specimen NHMUK PV R 1111, would be the new lectotype of Scelidosaurus

facts.statement: The new lectotype skeleton was found in the Black Ven Marl or Woodstone Nodule Bed, which are marine deposits of the Charmouth Mudstone Formation.
facts.quote: The new lectotype skeleton had been uncovered in the Black Ven Marl or Woodstone Nodule Bed, marine deposits of the Charmouth Mudstone Formation

facts.statement: The Scelidosaurus fossils date to the late Sinemurian stage, approximately 191 million years ago.
facts.quote: dating from the late Sinemurian stage, about 191 million years ago

facts.statement: The lectotype skeleton is nearly complete, missing only the snout tip, neck base, forelimbs, and tail end.
facts.quote: It consists of a rather complete skeleton with skull and lower jaws. Only the snout tip, the neck base, the forelimbs and the tail end are missing

facts.statement: Hundreds of osteoderms were found associated with the skeleton, many in their original positions.
facts.quote: Hundreds of osteoderms were found in connection with the skeleton, many more or less in their original position

facts.statement: Richard Owen suggested in 1861 that Scelidosaurus was a fish-eater that partially lived in the sea, a view that differs from modern ideas.
facts.quote: Owen in 1861 suggested a lifestyle for Scelidosaurus that is very different from present ideas: it would have been a fish-eater and partially sea-dwelling

facts.statement: It is debated whether the misidentified knee joint belongs to Scelidosaurus or to a member of the Coelophysoidea or Neoceratosauria.
facts.quote: It more likely belongs to some member of the Coelophysoidea or Neoceratosauria

facts.statement: David Bruce Norman published new articles on the skull and postcrania of Scelidosaurus in 2020.
facts.quote: In 2020, Norman published articles on the skull and the postcrania, also taking later finds into account

facts.statement: In 1888, R. Lydekker cataloged numerous single bones, mostly limb elements and osteoderms, acquired by the Natural History Museum, London, from the Norris collection.
facts.quote: In 1888 Lydekker catalogued a large number of single bones, largely limb elements, and osteoderms, that had been acquired by the NHMUK from the Norris collection.

facts.statement: In 1861, Richard Owen described a second partial juvenile skeleton of Scelidosaurus, now registered as specimen LYMPH 1997.37.4-10 in the Lyme Regis Museum.
facts.quote: Owen in 1861 described a second, partial, skeleton of a juvenile animal, that later was added to the collection of Elizabeth Philpot and today is registered in the Lyme Regis Museum as specimen LYMPH 1997.37.4-10.

facts.statement: A second partial juvenile skeleton, specimen NHMUK PV R6704, was formally described in 1968, though it had been reported as early as 1959.
facts.quote: In 1968 a second partial juvenile skeleton was described, specimen NHMUK PV R6704, that had already been reported in 1959.

facts.statement: In 1985, Simon Barnsley, David Costain, and Peter Langham excavated a partial skeleton with a complete skull and skin impressions, now registered as specimen BRSMG CE12785 in the Bristol Museum.
facts.quote: In 1985 Simon Barnsley, David Costain and Peter Langham excavated a partial skeleton including a very complete skull and skin impressions, which was sold to the Bristol Museum where it is registered as specimen BRSMG CE12785.

facts.statement: David Sole found a 3.1-meter-long skeleton in 2000, which may be the most complete non-avian dinosaur specimen ever discovered in the British Isles, though it remains undescribed.
facts.quote: Several specimens remain undescribed because they are in private collections. These include a 3.1 metres (ten feet) long skeleton found by David Sole in 2000, perhaps the most complete non-avian dinosaur exemplar ever discovered in the British Isles.

facts.statement: Between 1980 and 2000, palaeontologist Roger Byrne discovered three fossils on a beach near The Gobbins in Northern Ireland.
facts.quote: Between the years 1980 and 2000, three fossils were discovered on a beach near The Gobbins in Northern Ireland by palaeontologist Roger Byrne.

facts.statement: Roger Byrne's finds include a femur fragment (BELUM K3998) found in January 1980, a tibia fragment (BELUM K12493) found in April 1981, and a pentagonal object (BELUM K2015.1.54) found in 2000.
facts.quote: The specimens include BELUM K3998, a proximal femur fragment discovered in January 1980; BELUM K12493, the fragment of a tibia shaft discovered in April 1981; and BELUM K2015.1.54, a small pentagonal object discovered in 2000.

facts.statement: In 1989, histologist Robin Reid identified a femur fragment as dinosaurian based on bone texture and structure, suggesting it belonged to Scelidosaurus or a similar animal.
facts.quote: Histologist Robin Reid recognized the first specimen as dinosaurian due to its bone texture and structure, and reported it in 1989, suspecting it belonged to Scelidosaurus or a similar animal.

facts.statement: In 2024, Satchell reidentified the femur fragment BELUM K3998 as an indeterminate dinosaur remain, excluding it from Scelidosaurus or Ornithischia.
facts.quote: However, in 2024, Satchell reidentified the proximal femur fragment (BELUM K3998) as an indeterminate dinosaur remain, not belonging to a Scelidosaurus or an ornithischian.

facts.statement: Specimen BRSMG CF2781, containing preserved soft tissue, was discovered in the early 1990s in the legacy of Professor John Challinor, who used it for lectures.
facts.quote: The fossil, with inventory number BRSMG CF2781, was in the early 1990s, in an already prepared state, discovered in the legacy of the late Professor John Challinor, who had used it to illustrate his lectures.

facts.statement: Scelidosaurus harrisonii, named and described by Owen, is the only currently recognized species of Scelidosaurus.
facts.quote: Scelidosaurus harrisonii, named and described by Owen, is currently the only recognized species, based on several nearly complete skeletons.

facts.statement: David Jay Simmons described fossils from the Sinemurian-age Lower Lufeng Formation as a potential second species, Scelidosaurus oehleri, in 1965, initially placing it in the genus Tatisaurus.
facts.quote: A potential second species from the Sinemurian-age Lower Lufeng Formation, Scelidosaurus oehleri, was described by David Jay Simmons in 1965 under its own genus, Tatisaurus.

facts.statement: Spencer G. Lucas reassigned S. oehleri to Scelidosaurus in 1996, but this view is not accepted, and the species is now recognized as Tatisaurus.
facts.quote: In 1996 Spencer G. Lucas moved it to Scelidosaurus. Although the fossils are fragmentary, this reassessment has not been accepted, and S. oehleri is today once again recognized as Tatisaurus.

facts.statement: The Sole skeleton differs from the lectotype in armor details, leading to debate over whether it represents a separate taxon or sexual dimorphism.
facts.quote: The finds by Sole differ from the lectotype in details of the armour and might represent a separate taxon or reflect sexual dimorphism.

facts.statement: Norman rejected the hypothesis that the Sole skeleton represents a separate taxon or reflects sexual dimorphism.
facts.quote: Norman denied this.

facts.statement: Subsequent studies reinterpreted the Irish tibia as belonging to an indeterminate neotheropod, the pentagonal object as basalt, and Grey's specimen as an ichthyosaur.
facts.quote: However, the tibia was reinterpreted as that of an indeterminate neotheropod, the pentagonal object as a mere piece of basalt resembling a fossil, and Grey's specimen as belonging to an ichthyosaur.

facts.statement: Scientists rejected the assignment of Arizona scutes to Scelidosaurus because the scutes differ in form.
facts.quote: Later scientists have rejected the assignment to Scelidosaurus, as the scutes are different in form.

facts.statement: Roman Ulansky named S. arizonenesis in 2014, but Peter Malcolm Galton and Kenneth Carpenter identified it as a nomen dubium in 2016, placing the specimens as indeterminate Thyreophora.
facts.quote: In 2014, Roman Ulansky named a new species, S. arizonenesis, based on these specimens. In 2016, Peter Malcolm Galton and Kenneth Carpenter identified it as a nomen dubium, instead once again placing the specimens as Thyreophora indet.

facts.statement: Richard Owen speculated that Scelidosaurus might have been ovoviviparous due to its relatively large size and presumed marine lifestyle.
facts.quote: As it was relatively large, Owen speculated, in the context of its presumed marine lifestyle, that Scelidosaurus might have been ovoviviparous.

facts.statement: The short, backward-pointing pubis in the juvenile specimen convinced scientists that it was not the main pubic body, challenging earlier beliefs about its homology with the forward-pointing pubis in most reptiles.
facts.quote: The short prepubis in this specimen convinced scientists that this process did not represent the main pubic body as some had thought, who had been unable to believe that the thin, backward-pointing, pubis with the Ornithischia was homologous to the forward-pointing much larger pubic bone in most reptilian groups.

facts.statement: Researchers concluded that the osteoderms of basal armored dinosaurs, including Scelidosaurus, were covered in a tough, likely keratinous layer of skin.
facts.quote: The authors concluded that the osteoderms of all basal armoured dinosaurs were covered in a tough, probably keratinous layer of skin.

facts.statement: A partial juvenile skeleton found in Charmouth dates to the early Pliensbachian, approximately 190 million years ago.
facts.quote: Found by geologist James Frederick Jackson (1894–1966) of Charmouth, it is from a slightly younger layer, the Stonebarrow Marl Member dating to the early Pliensbachian, about 190 million years old.

facts.statement: A specimen with preserved soft tissue, consisting of eight caudal vertebrae, dates from the late Hettangian to Sinemurian stages.
facts.quote: Its provenance is unknown. It consists of a series of eight caudal vertebrae in a cut slab of carbonate mudstone, which was judged to date from the late Hettangian to Sinemurian stages.

facts.statement: Scutes from the Kayenta Formation were initially used to date the strata to 199.6-196.5 million years ago, based on the assumption that Scelidosaurus harrisonii dated to the early Sinemurian.
facts.quote: Kevin Padian referred to a Scelidosaurus sp., and used to determine that the age of the strata was around 199.6-196.5 million years ago, at a time when it was still thought that Scelidosaurus harrisonii dated to the early Sinemurian.

facts.statement: Sir Richard Owen described Scelidosaurus in 1859 based on initial findings from the 1850s.
facts.quote: Después de los hallazgos iniciales en la década de 1850, el anatomista comparativo Sir Richard Owen describió a Scelidosaurus en 1859.

facts.statement: Scelidosaurus lived on the supercontinent Laurasia during its time.
facts.quote: Este género y los otros relacionados de ese momento vivían en el supercontinente Laurasia.

facts.statement: Scelidosaurus was a lightly armored, quadrupedal herbivore reaching about 4 meters in length.
facts.quote: Era un herbívoro cuadrúpedo, ligeramente acorazado que alcanzaba los 4 metros de largo.

facts.statement: Scelidosaurus had light armor consisting of long horizontal rows of keeled oval shields extending along the neck, back, and tail.
facts.quote: Scelidosaurus tenía una armadura ligera, protegido por largas filas horizontales de escudos ovalados con quillas que se extendían a lo largo del cuello, lomo y cola.

facts.statement: Some scientists have estimated the length of Scelidosaurus at 4 meters.
facts.quote: Algunos científicos lo han estimado con una longitud de 4 metros.

facts.statement: In 2010, Gregory S. Paul estimated Scelidosaurus had a body length of 3.8 meters and a weight of 270 kilograms.
facts.quote: En 2010, Gregory S. Paul dio una longitud corporal de 3,8 metros (12,5 pies) y un peso de 270 kilogramos.

facts.statement: Scelidosaurus was quadrupedal with hind limbs considerably longer than the front limbs.
facts.quote: Scelidosaurus era cuadrúpedo, con los miembros traseros considerablemente más largos que los delanteros.

facts.statement: Scelidosaurus had a small, elongated head used to bite low plants and shrubs, which were then processed in large intestines.
facts.quote: cuyas partes eran mordidas por la cabeza pequeña y alargada para ser procesadas en los grandes intestinos.

facts.statement: Scelidosaurus may have reared up on its hind legs to browse tree foliage, but its front feet were as large as its hind feet, indicating a primarily quadrupedal posture.
facts.quote: Pudo haberse levantado sobre sus patas traseras para hojear sobre el follaje de los árboles, pero sus pies delanteros eran tan grandes como sus pies traseros, indicando una postura sobre todo cuadrúpeda.

facts.statement: A trackway in the Holy Cross Mountains of Poland shows a Scelidosaurus-like animal walking bipedally, suggesting it may have been more competent at bipedalism than previously thought.
facts.quote: Un sendero de las montañas Holy Cross de Polonia muestra un animal parecido a un Scelidosaurus caminando de manera bípeda, lo que sugiere que pudo haber sido más competente en el bipedalismo de lo que se pensaba anteriormente.

facts.statement: Owen placed Scelidosaurus in the Dinosauria in 1861.
facts.quote: Scelidosaurus was placed in the Dinosauria by Owen in 1861.

facts.statement: Thomas Henry Huxley validly named the family Scelidosauridae in 1869, after Edward Drinker Cope's proposal was only published in December 1871.
facts.quote: In 1868/1869 Edward Drinker Cope proposed a family Scelidosauridae in a double lecture but this was only published in December 1871; therefore it was Thomas Henry Huxley who validly named the Scelidosauridae in 1869.

facts.statement: Today, paleontologists usually consider Scelidosauridae paraphyletic, though Benton (2004) lists it as monophyletic.
facts.quote: Today, paleontologists usually consider the Scelidosauridae paraphyletic, thus not forming a separate branch or clade; however, Benton (2004) lists the group as monophyletic.

facts.statement: Most evidence today indicates that Scelidosaurus is the sister taxon to the two main clades of Thyreophora, Stegosauria and Ankylosauria.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Scelidosaurus is a true ankylosaur closely related to ankylosaurids or basal to the split between ankylosaurs and stegosaurs.

facts.statement: The exact position of Scelidosaurus within the suborder has been a subject of debate for nearly 150 years.
facts.quote: Al ser uno de los tireofóros más primitivos, la ubicación exacta de Scelidosaurus dentro del suborden ha sido un tema de debate por cerca de 150 años.

facts.statement: A fully grown Scelidosaurus was relatively small compared to most other dinosaurs but was of medium size for the Early Jurassic.
facts.quote: Un Scelidosaurus totalmente crecido era más bien pequeño, comparado con la mayoría de otros dinosaurios, pero era una especie de tamaño mediano en el Jurásico temprano.

facts.statement: Scelidosaurus had four toes on each foot, with the inner digit being the smallest.
facts.quote: Scelidosaurus tenía cuatro dedos en cada pie, siendo el dígito interior el más pequeño.

facts.statement: The skull of Scelidosaurus was low and triangular in shape, longer than it was wide, similar to early ornithischians.

facts.statement: The head of Scelidosaurus was small, approximately 20 centimeters long, and elongated.
facts.quote: La cabeza de Scelidosaurus era pequeña, de unos 20 centímetros de largo y alargada.

facts.statement: Scelidosaurus retained five pairs of cranial fenestrae, a feature seen in primitive ornithischians.
facts.quote: Scelidosaurus todavía tenía los cinco pares de fenestras , aberturas del cráneo, vista en ornitisquios primitivos

facts.statement: The teeth of Scelidosaurus were longer and more triangular in lateral view compared to later armored dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Sus dientes eran más largos y más triangulares en vista lateral que en los dinosaurios blindados posteriores.

facts.statement: There were at least five teeth in each premaxilla, at least nineteen in the maxilla, and sixteen in the dentary of the lower jaw.
facts.quote: Había al menos cinco dientes en cada premaxilar, y al menos diecinueve en el maxilar y dieciséis en el dentario de la mandíbula inferior.

facts.statement: In 2020, Norman concluded that a specific bone was a fused palpebral bone.
facts.quote: En 2020, Norman concluyó que se trataba de un hueso palpebral fusionado.

facts.statement: The epivomeres, special bones covering the roof of the nasal cavity, are not known from any other animal.
facts.quote: No se conocen de ningún otro animal.

facts.statement: Like other thyreophorans, Scelidosaurus was a herbivore with small, leaf-shaped molar teeth suitable for shredding vegetation.
facts.quote: Como otros tireóforos, Scelidosaurus era herbívoro, con los dientes malares muy pequeños, foliformes convenientes para desmenuzar la vegetación.

facts.statement: It is believed that Scelidosaurus fed by crushing food between its teeth using a simple up-and-down jaw movement.
facts.quote: Se cree Scelidosaurus se alimentaba con sistema de en el que el alimento entre los dientes era machacado con un movimiento de arriba abajo simple de las quijadas.

facts.quote: PBDB name: Scelidosaurus (genus), Owen 1859

facts.statement: The parent group of Scelidosaurus is Scelidosauridae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Scelidosauridae

facts.statement: Scelidosaurus is classified in the class Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Class: Ornithischia

facts.statement: Scelidosaurus lived from the Rhaetian to the Toarcian, between 205.7 and 174.7 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Rhaetian to Toarcian (205.7 to 174.7 million years ago)

facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 13
